title: Born of the Virgin (CCC 496–507)
hook: the Church professes Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ and Lord: Christ from the Greek for Messiah, Lord the word once kept for God. Your line was anointed. Where did you hear that title yesterday? Day one thousand seventy-four.

A virgin in Nazareth, betrothed to a man named Joseph, has just been told she will have a son, and that he will be great, and called the Son of the most High. Luke gives her one question, and it's a practical one. In the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" She isn't asking for a sign. She's asking how. And the angel's answer is the center of today: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee." The Apostles' Creed folds that whole scene into a few words: born of the Virgin Mary. Today's word names what the Church means by them.
screen: `A VIRGIN IN NAZARETH.` → `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` → `THE HOLY GHOST SHALL COME UPON THEE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism states the teaching directly. The Church confesses that Jesus was conceived solely by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary, with no human father. Luke tells it from Mary's side; Matthew tells it from Joseph's. In Matthew, Joseph finds Mary with child, and being a just man, he plans to send her away quietly. Then an angel in a dream tells him that what is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost, and he takes her home as his wife. The Catechism is honest that this isn't an easy teaching. It notes that people have objected, and that some have called it a legend. Its reply is not a proof. It says the Gospels present this as God's own work, beyond human understanding, and that its meaning opens up only to faith. So what does it mean, in Catholic teaching? First, that the beginning is God's. Jesus has only God as his Father; the initiative is entirely from above. Second, that something new is starting. The Catechism calls Jesus the new Adam, the start of a new creation. Third, it's a sign for everyone else: a new birth by the Spirit, which Catholics connect with baptism. One clarification is worth carrying home tonight. This is not the same as the Immaculate Conception. The virginal conception is about how Jesus was conceived. The Immaculate Conception is a different teaching, about Mary herself, kept free from original sin from the first moment of her own life. Different teaching. And Mary's last line in Luke's scene is the one the Angelus repeats: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
screen: `CONCEIVED BY THE HOLY SPIRIT ALONE.` · `LUKE FROM MARY'S SIDE, MATTHEW JOSEPH'S.` · `GOD'S WORK, OPEN TO FAITH.` · `NOT THE IMMACULATE CONCEPTION.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The Angelus is an old Catholic prayer, by tradition said when a church bell rings. It walks through this very scene: the angel's message, Mary's answer, and the Word made flesh, with a Hail Mary between. If you pray and know it, you can pray it now, slowly. If you don't know it, or don't pray, settle and breathe, and stay with Mary's answer instead: be it done to me according to thy word. Notice how it feels to say yes to something you can't fully see. The bell holds the time.
Virginal conception. The Church's teaching that Jesus was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in Mary's womb, with no human father. Not the Immaculate Conception. Today's word.
Your line: by the holy spirit. Today, if a bell rings, a church bell, a timer, a phone, let it remind you of Mary's practical question, and her answer. Day one thousand seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the virginal conception in the Creed at Mass, and some pray the Angelus, a short prayer on the Annunciation said traditionally at morning, noon and evening.

CCC paraphrased: conceived solely by the Holy Spirit (496), God's work beyond understanding (497), objections and 'accessible only to faith' (498), only God as Father (503), new Adam (504), sign of new birth (505). Immaculate Conception distinction from CCC 490–491 (outside the day's range; added to prevent a common confusion).
Practice describes the Angelus (three versicles with a Hail Mary after each; morning, noon and evening) without quoting it. Confirm the description.
Feast claim cut under the claims rule.
Original: παρθένος (Luke 1:27 has the accusative παρθένον). Keeper may prefer null.
Carry is lowercase 'by the holy spirit' as in the index; the voice says Holy Ghost only inside Douay-Rheims quotations.

Editor: 'young woman' became Luke's 'virgin, betrothed'; the Creed line is attributed to the Apostles' Creed (the Nicene wording at Mass differs); 'never been an easy teaching' softened; cut the uncited feast claim and the Angelus counts (three verses, three times a day).
Audit: cut the unsourced superlative that the Church keeps Mary's answer 'closest'; it is now tied to the Angelus, which the practice describes. Luke 1:34, 35, 38 Challoner wording checked.
